BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Low pressure will stay southeast of the region for the weekend, allowing a short-lived ridge of high pressure to build in and bring dry conditions and a slight warming trend through Sunday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A chance of showers will spread northward into the area tonight, then become widespread Thursday and Thursday night, along with a chance of thunderstorms.
- Thunderstorms Thursday afternoon into evening will be capable of isolated severe wind gusts/hail in Southwest Idaho.
- Becoming windy late Thursday night behind a cold front, with much cooler conditions Friday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Upper low off central California is forecast to move inland across southern California Thursday morning, then northeastward through Nevada later Thursday, and into southern Idaho by Friday morning, an ideal track for rain in our CWA. Latest models have more QPF than the previous cycle, especially in Idaho, and we have issued a Flash Flood Watch for the Wapiti and Crooked Burn Scars for Thursday night and Friday morning. WPC has a marginal risk of excessive rainfall in our CWA Thursday and Thursday night. At that time lift will be enhanced by a surface cold front, and instability will increase ahead of the incoming upper low, as also indicated by SPC's thunderstorm forecast. We estimate total rainfall through Friday at 1.00 to 1.25 inch in Idaho north of the Snake Basin, .50 to .75 inch in the Snake Basin, and .35 to .60 inch in eastern OR. These values are about double what models showed yesterday. Rainfall should also last longer, well into Friday on the Idaho side, but ending from west to east in Oregon as colder and drier air comes in behind the cold front. Rain may briefly change to snow before ending in Harney County Friday morning.

Later Friday part of the upper low will continue to move north- eastward and join up with a trough moving across western Canada, while the rest of the low splits southward and moves to Arizona. Our CWA will then dry out and become significantly colder, with low temps Saturday morning in the teens and 20s in the mountains and lower to mid 30s in the valleys, while high temps stay only in the upper 40s and 50s.

Winds will stay light through Thursday morning, then increase from the southeast Thursday afternoon, especially in and south of the Snake Basin. Gusts to 35 mph will develop between Boise and Twin Falls Thursday afternoon. Winds will shift to west or northwest Thursday night behind the cold front, and continue 15 to 25 mph with gusts to 35 mph Friday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Low pressure will stay southeast of the region for the weekend, allowing a short-lived ridge of high pressure to build in and bring dry conditions and a slight warming trend through Sunday. Temperatures will climb to about 5-10 degrees above normal for Sunday and Monday, with cooler and wetter conditions returning thanks to a Gulf of Alaska low pressure system moving inland from the northeastern Pacific. Lingering forecast uncertainty exists for the timing and track of this low pressure system, with disagreement present in ensemble solutions and between deterministic models. Current forecast shows this cut off low bringing much cooler, below normal temperatures and a 30-50% chance of precipitation over higher terrain from Tuesday to late Wednesday. Snow levels will likely range from 5500-6500 feet, depending on the track of the low pressure, with light mountain snow accumulation by early Thursday.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Following the system a ridge builds in behind it. Clearing skies and a gradual warming trend. The next storm system is being advertised in the GFS, however there are significant run to run variability in the timing and positioning of this system.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above average temperatures will continue through the end of the week, but a weekend system will drop temperatures towards near to below-average.
- Precipitation possible Friday through Sunday, with the potential for frozen precipitation outside of the mountains on Sunday.
- Some clearing and warming back to near normal temperatures next week, with some low end precipitation chances mostly in the high terrain.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The overall pattern through Thursday night should remain largely unchanged as our region will sit between two stout systems, with a deep upper level ridge over the Central US, and a deep upper level Pacific low moving inland and then slowly northeastwards. This will continue to produce a southwesterly flow that will increase moisture across the region, particularly later into Thursday and moving into the weekend. For the rest of this evening and overnight, increasing cloudiness is seen on satellite primarily across Carbon and Albany Counties where the highest influx of moisture is moving in for the day. We could see a few light showers across this area, and some earlier runs of CAMs were producing even a weak echo as far east as Laramie County, but overall probabilities are on the low side alongside low confidence.

Cloudiness will overspread the region on Thursday though as the moisture continues to increase. While this could impact afternoon highs for the western half of the forecast area, 700 mb temperatures remain at around 7-10 C which should encourage highs similar to today in the 60's to 70's. CAMs are much more excited for precipitation extending out of the high terrain tomorrow afternoon and evening, with a chance of showers across much of the I-80 corridor through Nebraska. While storm chances are largely declining as we enter the cold season, a brief swath of CAPE around 200-300 J/kg across Carbon County could encourage a rumble of thunder or two, but don't expect much out of this activity. Otherwise cloudiness should linger through the nighttime hours which will allow for overnight lows to remain on the warm side due to insulation, with upper 40's to 50's across eastern Wyoming and the Nebraska panhandle as we move into the weekend.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: On Friday the upper level Pacific system will be approaching from the southwest. Ahead of it a few impulses of mid and low level vorticity are progged to pass over the area, allowing showers to exist over mostly the intermountain areas. In addition, a jet streak of about 80-100 knots intensifies ahead of the system. The phase of the jet and impulses are somewhat mistimed to allow for more widespread precipitation. The jet will suppress the development of precipitation due to a healthy amount of positive omega below 500 mbar. The exceptions are in the Nebraska Panhandle where the entrance region of the jet may be more favorable. It also helps that this region will have more moisture and instability to work with. Skew-T profiles have about 500 MUCAPE and 60 knots of speed shear to perhaps prop up a few thunderstorms at and after peak daytime heating. No severe weather is anticipated with any storm, though small hail is a probability given the shear. The clearing cloud coverage to the east allows much of the Panhandle to reach the mid 70 to low 80s in the afternoon. Moving west, the cloud coverage increases, only allowing southeast Wyoming to make it into the mid 60s to low 70s. Overnight a cold front is expected to make its way southeast through the area. A 10 degree drop from Thursday overnight lows is likely, with lows in the mid 30s to low 40s.

Returning to the upper level system to our west. The evolution through Friday is for the trough to split and elongate. The northern portion gets picked up by a strong negatively tilted trough in Canada, while the southern end of the trough remains over the southwest. This southern lobe of the system will be the driver of more exciting weather going into Sunday and Monday.

Post front Saturday is anticipated to be breezy and partly to mostly cloudy. Winds behind the front could be fresh with gusts to 40 mph possible. A few showers are possible as they drift north from the advection activity in Colorado, but otherwise a dry day. Temperatures struggle to make it to 60, with most of us staying in the 50s. Sunday the remaining Pacific system moves northeast bringing with it more chances for precipitation. The GFS is picking up on a possible TROWL setting up over our northern counties. Temperatures are marginal for any accumulation of snow, but a mix of snow and rain at the surface is possible. At our peaks an inch or two of snow may be possible.

Following the system a ridge builds in behind it. Clearing skies and a gradual warming trend. The next storm system is being advertised in the GFS, however there are significant run to run variability in the timing and positioning of this system. The ECMWF is telling a similar story, although the system is much flatter and slower. Precipitation chances would be on the lower side with this system with not much synoptically to refill the moisture reserve ahead of the trough and not much attendant with the airmass associated with it.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: These conditions look to change overnight into tomorrow as we come more under the influence of the trough to the west cooling the air aloft to provide some CAPE to support convection.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widespread rain continues tomorrow through early Friday.
- Strong to severe thunderstorms will be possible favoring southeastern Utah and far Western Colorado generally from I-70 south Thursday and Thursday night.
- The potential for flooding increases Thursday and Friday, especially for portions of southeast Utah and southwest Colorado.
- Rainfall amounts in the southern mountains range from 1-3 inches with higher amounts of 2-4" or more possible in the San Juans and southern foothills.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A deep trough off the West Coast and High pressure to the southeast near Big Bend is keeping the Desert Southwest under a strong south to southwesterly flow aloft advecting deep subtropical moisture north through Arizona into eastern Utah and Western Colorado. Models are in good agreement with satellite imagery showing the low just turning the corner in the base of the trough off the SoCal Coast before ejecting to the northeast into the Great Basin Thursday evening and continuing into Montana Friday evening taking most of the moisture with it. Meanwhile, another shortwave system descending into the trough Friday cuts off over SoCal Friday night to eject farther east over the region Saturday night into Sunday to keep unsettled weather in the forecast through the weekend. Models stay in fairly good agreement through the weekend, but are diverging on the timing and track of the second system by Sunday with some solutions tracking it to the west over northern Utah. The models do generally agree on setting up a dry zonal flow across the region next week that could extend into the next weekend, but that a long way out and confidence is lot on the extended period.

Today we saw quieter showers with rain rates remaining on the low side only around a half inch per hour in the heavier showers. Even though we had strong vertical sheer and plenty moisture on hand, with all the heavy cloud cover and the warm air aloft, we just didn't have any CAPE to feed stronger storms. Both the 18Z and 00Z soundings showed a saturated atmosphere nearly up to 200mb for efficient rain making, but with zero CAPE there wasn't the strong convection. That being said, much of the southern half of the region still received an inch or more rain today saturating the soil with water and priming the area for flash flooding should heavier showers come overnight into tomorrow.

These conditions look to change overnight into tomorrow as we come more under the influence of the trough to the west cooling the air aloft to provide some CAPE to support convection. Additionally, upper- level dynamics increase as a 70-90 kt jet moves in over the region. The primary concern with convection will be strong winds over 60 mph possible as the winds aloft mix down. The atmosphere remains saturated through the day, making localized heavy rain in showers and thunderstorms much more likely leading to flash flooding, especially near recent fire scars and areas prone to flooding like slot canyons and steep terrain. Stay tuned to the forecast for updates as weather develops through the day. Drier air starts moving into the region late tomorrow which looks to scatter out the showers and thunderstorms, but also looks to increase the potential for stronger thunderstorms overnight into Friday. Most of the moisture is swept out of the region Friday limiting convective activity through the afternoon, but has the second low starts moving in from the west, showers and thunderstorms will pick up again Friday night into Saturday feeding on the residual moisture and continue through Saturday night and Sunday as the low tracks over the region. The storms move on off to the east as a zonal pattern sets up across the region Sunday night through mid next week.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Monday through Wednesday...Upper low weekend, opens and tracks east across CO as an open wave on Monday, with just some lingering isolated to low end scattered showers across the CWA.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Flood Watch remains in effect through Friday afternoon for the eastern San Juan mountains and the Upper Rio Grande Valley, with stream/river flooding and rock/mud slides possible.
- Periods of moderate to heavy rain for the Continental Divide, focusing on the San Juan Range through Friday, with the heaviest amounts forecast for today.
- Generally warm across the plains through Friday, then much cooler and unsettled this weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...Pacific low sitting just off the CA coast late tonight is certainly bringing the advertised moisture to western CO, with 12 hr rainfall amounts as of 11 pm at around .5 to 1.0 inch across the sw mts, and .2 to .4 of an inch across the rest of the higher terrain. Some isolated showers have pushed across the I-25 corridor but so far have just amounted to generally a trace. Overnight low temps are forecast to drop into the 40s for the high valleys, and upper 40s to mid 50s for the plains.

Today and tonight...Everything is still pointing to today as seeing the greatest impacts from this Pacific storm. The upper low moves onshore and across CA and into NV through the day today, then shifts north across northern NV tonight. At the same time, an upper shortwave rotates around the low across AZ today, sweeping across western CO this evening. While deep moist southwest flow will persist across the Four Corners through the day and night, this shortwave will provide the upper dynamic support late this afternoon and evening for increased rainfall amounts and rates. At the same time, another upper low breaks off from the main feature and strengthens over southern CA - more on that later. WPC has painted much of western CO, all the way to the Sangres, under a Slight area for excessive rainfall, and has a Moderate area that encompasses much of southwestern CO including the sw mts. Therefore, plan on periods of moderate rainfall through the first half of the day today along the Continental Divide, then becoming periods of heavier rainfall expected late this aftn and eve, especially across the sw mts.

The focus area continues to be the southwest mts, with total additional rainfall amounts there through the day today ranging from 2 to 3 inches, while the remainder of the Continental Divide and the Sangres could see an additional half inch to an inch of rain. The San Luis Valley and the Upper Arkansas River Valley will likely receive another .25 to .5 of an inch of moisture. Periods of heavier rainfall falling on already saturated ground will lead to excessive runoff and perhaps rock/mud slides. Given what has already fallen across the area Wed, these forecast additional amounts add up to totals being on the high end of original storm estimates.

Those living or traveling across the southwest mountains should stay weather aware today and tomorrow, and have multiple ways to receive weather warnings. As for the eastern plains, continued warm conditions anticipated with some isolated shower activity spreading across the I-25 Corridor possible. Look for highs in the 50s to around 60F for the high valleys, and 70s to lower 80s for the plains.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Friday...As the main upper low continues pushing to the north through the day, another piece of energy separates and drops south across southern CA, becoming a secondary closed low over southern CA and AZ. As this is occurring, strong southwest support for rainfall across western CO drops off so rainfall rates decrease dramatically, and the Flood Watch will be allowed to expire at 00z Sat. Colder air pushes in, dropping snow levels through the night. The northern low continues east as an open trough, forcing a cold front south across eastern WY. Rain totals of an additional .40 of an inch for the eastern San Juans, and up to a tenth of an inch elsewhere, are forecast, then showers and isolated thunderstorms push along the southern border and up across the far southeast corner through the late afternoon and evening. This will be the last really warm day for the eastern plains as temps once again climb into the 70s to around 80F, while the high valleys climb into the 60s.

Saturday and Sunday...A cold front pushes south into eastern CO Saturday morning, while the southern closed low moves up across AZ and reaches the Four Corners by Sat night. This will produce strong south to southwest flow, this time situated across the eastern half of the state. Widespread showers and thunderstorms are expected on Saturday, with excessive rainfall amounts possible for the eastern plains, and new accumulating snow for the mts as snow levels drop to around 9500 ft late that night. On Sunday the upper low starts to open up and track east into CO, continuing to bring rain and storm chances to the plains, while snow chances start to diminish. Plan on much cooler temps both days, with highs in the 50s for the high valleys, and 50s to lower 60s for the plains.

Monday through Wednesday...Upper low weekend, opens and tracks east across CO as an open wave on Monday, with just some lingering isolated to low end scattered showers across the CWA. Temporary broad ridging aloft then develops across the region for Tuesday and Wednesday. Monday looks to be another very cool day, then a gradual warming trend into midweek with temps climbing back up to seasonal normals. Moore

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Weak ridging is then expected to move over Utah and southwest Wyoming to start the upcoming work week, bringing a bit of warming to the area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widespread precipitation will bring an elevated and prolonged threat of flash flooding across southern and central Utah through Thursday. There is a Slight Risk of excessive rainfall (level 2 of 4) across southern Utah on Thursday.
- There is a Marginal Risk (level 1 of 5) for severe thunderstorms is in place across southern and western Utah on Thursday.

- The late week storm will also bring accumulating snowfall to the high terrain across northern and central Utah on Friday, with 1-4" likely above 9000 feet. There is a chance of locally higher amounts for favored locations.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The center of a broad closed low is approaching the California coast this evening, with Utah and southwest Wyoming under a southerly flow out ahead of it. This has allowed deep tropical moisture to move into the forecast area, with satellite derived PWs primarily in the 0.6 to 0.7 inch range, which is above the 90th percentile for PW for this time of year. The position of the upper jet on the front side of the system has brought a good amount of instability, particularly for southwest Utah, with enough shear to promote some organized convection. One earlier storm produced golf ball size hail, but flash flooding has been the primary threat, and will continue to be through tomorrow.

Convection is currently in a relative lull, though at least some showers and thunderstorms will continue over southern Utah overnight. Meanwhile, the main low will move onshore tomorrow, splitting as it does so. One piece is expected to eject northward across Utah and southwest Wyoming late Thursday afternoon through early Friday with the other piece moving into northern Mexico. By the early afternoon, convection is expected to become more intense again over southern Utah, with the moisture and instability spreading northward into northern portions of the area with the movement of the trough. Conditions will remain quite favorable for flash flooding over central and southern Utah, and thus the Flood Watch remains in effect through early Friday.

As the trough moves through, it will bring colder air along with it, resulting in highs 5-10F below seasonal normals Friday afternoon. The colder air will also bring snow levels down to around 9,000 feet, bringing accumulating snow to the highest terrain of northern Utah, though most likely not significant amounts. Drier conditions will follow beginning Friday as the north piece of the trough ejects out of the area, but the presence of the southern branch of the low will keep temperatures on the cool side through the weekend. The southern branch of the system is also likely to bring a few showers to at least southeast Utah Saturday into Sunday as it tracks east across the Desert Southwest.

Weak ridging is then expected to move over Utah and southwest Wyoming to start the upcoming work week, bringing a bit of warming to the area. However, with no blocking ridge in place off the coast, the storm track is expected to remain active in some fashion next week, though there remains significant ensemble spread regard to the timing and details of any systems, along with their potential impacts for the forecast area.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: A moisture-laden storm arrives in Colorado on Wednesday, bringing early-season avalanche concerns to steep, snow-covered slopes. Nearly every fall, small avalanches catch eager snow riders, late-season hikers, and hunters off guard. If you are traveling through the high country over the next few days, exercise caution on steep, snow-covered terrain.

For Wednesday and Thursday, in areas with snow already on the ground, rain falling on the early snowpack increases the potential for Wet Loose avalanches. From Thursday through the weekend, as new snow accumulates and wind-drifted snow obscures the ground cover, dry slab and loose avalanches will become a threat at the highest elevations. It doesn't take much snow on steep grassy slopes, rock slabs, or remnant snowfields for slides to occur.
We will update the Statewide Avalanche Conditions as necessary. On November 1, 2026, we will resume our daily weather and avalanche forecasts.
We will update the Field Report and Avalanche Observations as information comes in, so please send us your observations.
An impressive tropical moisture stream takes aim at the Southern Mountains this week.

Wednesday & Thursday: During the early parts of the storm, precipitation will start as rain. Under specific storm cells dropping high-intensity precipitation and at the highest elevations, you can expect a few inches of snow by Thursday morning.

Thursday Night & Friday: A cold front will drop temperatures and snow levels. Expect 6 to 12+ inches of snow above treeline in the San Juan Mountains by Friday morning. The Central Mountains may see several inches in favored areas, with lighter accumulation further north.

Saturday through Monday: A closed low-pressure system crosses the Four Corners region, bringing additional snow. Depending on the storm's exact track, the Southern Mountains could see over 6 additional inches, while the Central and Northern Mountains can expect up to 6 inches.
The storm moves east on Tuesday, bringing a short-lived high-pressure ridge before another potential storm arrives for Halloween weekend.

You can get up-to-date point weather forecasts on our Weather Forecasts page by clicking on the map or searching for a location. You can also get model forecasts on our Point Forecasts page and Model Forecast page. You can check current weather conditions across Colorado on our Weather Stations page.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
